* fix(google_auth): persist oauth_client_path so refresh survives restart

Closes #72. The OAuth flow exchanged the auth code, saved the token, and
printed "Token saved successfully" — but never wrote oauth_client_path to
~/.config/claude-seo/google-api.json. On the next process start, when the

- New _persist_oauth_client_path(creds_path) helper. Reads existing config,
  sets oauth_client_path to the absolute path of client_secret.json,
  atomically writes via tempfile + os.replace. Merges (preserves api_key,
  service_account_path, ga4_property_id, etc.) — never clobbers.
- _exchange_code() takes creds_path and calls the helper after token save.
  Failure to persist warns to stderr but does not fail the auth flow.
- Both call sites (run_oauth_flow + --exchange CLI) pass creds_path through.

Security:
- Stores PATH only. client_secret value itself stays in client_secret.json
  on disk. Verified by unit test (Case 3 below).
- Atomic write avoids partial-write corruption if interrupted mid-flush.

- Case 1 fresh: oauth_client_path written to empty config
- Case 2 merge: existing api_key/service_account_path preserved
- Case 3 no leak: client_secret never appears in config file

  `parse_html()`'s output gains a `lazy_method` field alongside the
  existing `loading` field (backwards-compat: no field renamed/removed).

  per image. Do NOT flag "not lazy-loaded" when JS lazy-loaders are
  detected. They intentionally strip native `loading="lazy"` and use

fix(security): close DNS-rebinding via redirect target in _pin_dns

Self-audit during v2 review caught that _pin_dns only intercepted
getaddrinfo calls for the originally-pinned hostname. Redirect targets
following a 30x response (or any other host the request lifecycle
touched) fell through to the unpatched resolver with no IP validation.

Attack scenario:
  1. safe_requests_session('https://safe-public.com')
     -> _pin_dns pins safe-public.com to its validated public IP.
  2. safe-public.com responds 302 Location: https://evil.example/
  3. requests follows the redirect; getaddrinfo('evil.example')
     hits the original resolver (NOT pinned).
  4. evil.example's DNS returns 169.254.169.254 (AWS metadata IP).
  5. Connection proceeds; metadata leaks.

The same gap allowed an attacker controlling DNS for a domain the user
audited to redirect to any private IP. Severity: HIGH on a strict
reading (rebinding via redirect is the canonical SSRF chain), even
though exploitability requires aiming claude-seo at a malicious site.

Fix: in the patched getaddrinfo, the originally-pinned host still
returns the validated IP record directly (cheap, no resolution).
EVERY OTHER host gets resolved by the real getaddrinfo and then has
each returned A record checked against is_safe_ip. A single non-public
record fails the lookup with socket.gaierror, which requests surfaces
as ConnectionError — fetch_page already handles it as 'Connection error'.

This means the entire process-side resolver is SSRF-safe for the
duration of the pinned scope, not just one host. Side effect: any
unrelated localhost resolution inside the pinned scope will also fail,
which is desired (the scope is a critical section).

  - validate_url_strict DNS-resolving cases via unittest.mock.
  - _pin_dns: redirect target validation (the regression test for
    this bug), public passthrough, getaddrinfo restoration on normal
    and exceptional exits, concurrent-lock refusal.
  - make_safe_playwright_route_handler: continue/abort/data-URL
    paths, resource-type blocking, DNS-failure fail-closed.

fix(security): close obfuscated-IPv4 + FQDN + IPv6 + OAuth race bypasses

Second round of v2 self-audit closed four more exploitable issues in
the foundation. All four are now covered by regression tests.

1. Obfuscated IPv4 bypass in validate_url (HIGH)
---------------------------------------------------
validate_url() returned True for every glibc-accepted obfuscated form:
  http://127.0.0.001/      (leading zeros)
  http://2130706433/       (decimal integer)
  http://0x7f000001/       (hex integer)
  http://017700000001/     (octal integer)
  http://0177.0.0.1/       (octal dotted)
  http://0x7f.0.0.1/       (hex dotted)
  http://127.1/            (two-part shorthand)
  http://127.0.1/          (three-part shorthand)
Verified on Linux: socket.getaddrinfo() resolves every one of these
to 127.0.0.1. Any caller using validate_url() as a pre-flight gate
was vulnerable; validate_url_strict() caught them at DNS time but the
boolean form was the documented "parse-only" function.

Fix: new normalize_hostname() canonicalises via socket.inet_aton for
strings matching an IPv4 obfuscation regex. Used by both validate_url
and validate_url_strict so the two functions agree.

2. FQDN trailing-dot bypass of hostname blocklist (HIGH)
---------------------------------------------------
"metadata.google.internal." (trailing dot is RFC 1034 valid) and
"METADATA.GOOGLE.INTERNAL" (case variant) bypassed the exact-string
blocklist. On a GCP instance, both would have resolved to
169.254.169.254 — the strict mode caught it via IP check, but the
parse-only mode let it through.

Fix: normalize_hostname strips a single trailing dot and lowercases
before the blocklist lookup.

3. Playwright route handler IPv6 blind spot (MEDIUM)
---------------------------------------------------
make_safe_playwright_route_handler queried family=AF_INET only. A
hostname with public IPv4 + private IPv6 (fd00::1) would let the
route handler call continue_(); Chromium could then prefer IPv6 and
connect to the private address.

Fix: query AF_UNSPEC, validate every returned record (both families).
The handler also normalises the host first so obfuscated-IPv4 and
trailing-dot subresource requests are short-circuited before DNS.

4. OAuth save TOCTOU on file permissions (LOW)
---------------------------------------------------
The previous _save_oauth_token chmodded then opened — between the two
calls, an external process could replace the file, and os.open's
mode arg is silently ignored when the file already exists, leaving
the new write at the attacker's mode.

Fix: os.fchmod(fd, 0o600) on the open fd. Mode applied to the
descriptor we control regardless of whether the file pre-existed.

feat(content): detect templated title/description metadata

Adds scripts/metadata_template.py, a deterministic detector for
machine-generated title/description pairs, plus site-level roll-up.

The signature: a meta description that opens by restating its own
<title> verbatim and then closes with a stock call to action ("Try it
free now.", "Start free!", "Learn more now!"). Bulk metadata jobs — a
CSV column piped through a template, or an LLM asked for "a description
for each of these titles" — emit that exact shape on every URL of a site
at once, which is what makes it a scaled-content signal rather than a
copywriting nit.

Why this is worth a new check rather than a note in an existing one:
nothing in the repo currently compares a description against its title.
content_quality.py scores body text only; the seo-programmatic gate
measures unique body words per page; the seo-drift rules compare title
and description against their own past values, never against each other.
A site can pass every one of those while carrying one generated metadata
shape sitewide.

Incident this comes from: a live site was demoted by the June 2026
Google spam update for scaled content abuse. The cause was this exact
pattern across 26 pages, written by a bulk CSV metadata job. The body
copy was genuinely unique — average cross-page 8-gram Jaccard of 0.021 —
so every body-content heuristic passed, including a full claude-seo
audit run against the site, which did not surface the problem.

Detection is four string comparisons, no model and no inference about
authorship:

  templated_metadata            high    title echo + stock CTA tail
  description_echoes_title      medium  title echo, real content after
  brand_suffix_in_description   low     "| Brand" concatenated into body
  description_duplicates_title  medium  description == title

A CTA on its own never triggers anything: the description must also echo
the title. Titles below a normalised 25-character floor are exempt, so
short titles a sentence can legitimately open with ("Word Counter") stay
clean.

analyse_pairs() rolls single pages up to a site verdict and counts
repeated CTA tails, since one templated description is an oversight and
the same closing phrase on a third of the site is the pattern Google's
spam systems act on.

Wired into seo-page (single URL), the seo-content agent (audit path),
the quality-gates meta description table, and the seo-programmatic
uniqueness gate — the last because that gate explicitly measures body
copy, which is precisely how this slips through.

fix(matomo): route every request to the instance through url_safety

The PR shipped `_sanity_check_instance_url`, a deliberate SSRF bypass whose
docstring said it "intentionally does NOT use scripts/url_safety" because
self-hosted Matomo often sits on a private network. That reasoning was sound
before v2.3.0 and is obsolete after it: `CLAUDE_SEO_LOCAL_TARGETS` exists
precisely so a private, operator-owned target can be named without opening
the whole private range. A blanket bypass instead made `MATOMO_URL` a
general-purpose SSRF primitive, since the URL comes from settings a skill
can be talked into writing.

Every request to the instance now goes through `matomo_auth.post_to_instance`,
which uses `url_safety.safe_requests_session`: the endpoint is validated by
`validate_url_strict` (the one place that reads the allowlist) and pinned to
the validated address for the life of the session, so it cannot be re-bound
between validation and connect. The old function is now
`_normalize_instance_url` and does shape only (scheme, host, no userinfo),
because two SSRF policies in one tree is how the first one gets forgotten.

Redirects are refused rather than followed. The Reporting API answers a POST
with a JSON body; a 30x is either a misconfigured `MATOMO_URL` or an attempt
to pivot the pinned session onto another host, and the pin does not extend to
a redirect target. The error names the target host so the user can fix
`MATOMO_URL` themselves.

A private instance is reached by naming it in `CLAUDE_SEO_LOCAL_TARGETS`.
The refusal message carries the exact `host:port` line to add, both
installers print it at install time (`matomo_auth.py --local-target-hint`),
and the allowlist route is documented in MATOMO-SETUP.md, the SKILL.md, and
PRIVACY.md. The PRIVACY.md rows now say what is actually sent (idSite, the
report parameters, token_auth in the POST body) and that the bypass is gone.

Tests: public URL reaches the instance through the pinned session, private is
refused without the allowlist and accepted with it, an allowlist entry does
not open a neighbouring private host, a redirect to another host is refused,
and the token stays out of every envelope, exception string, and stream. The
transport stub now sits on the pinned session, and a module-level
`requests.post` raises, so a regression to an unguarded call fails loudly
instead of silently reaching the network.

Verified live against Matomo 5.13.0 in a local container: refused without the
allowlist, all seven subcommands green with it, and a real 302 to another host
refused.

fix(matomo): store the API token in ~/.config/claude-seo, not settings.json

The PR read `~/.config/claude-seo/matomo.json` with an environment fallback,
which is the right contract, but its installers never wrote that file. They
put `MATOMO_API_TOKEN` into `~/.claude/settings.json` under `env` instead.
settings.json is a general-purpose config file that tooling reads, prints,
diffs, and syncs, and it is not written with the guarded pattern the repo
already uses for API credentials.

`matomo_auth.save_config` now writes the credential file the loader already
reads, with the pattern from `backlinks_auth._write_secure_json`: pre-chmod an
existing file to close the legacy umask window, force 0600 on the open fd to
defeat the exists()/open() TOCTOU race, and a best-effort `icacls` pass on
Windows where mode bits are a no-op. On top of that the write is atomic. The
token goes to a same-directory temp file that is 0600 from creation, is
fsynced, and is then `os.replace`d into position, so an interrupted install
leaves the previous credentials intact rather than a truncated file, and a
concurrent reader never sees a partial one. The uninstaller's settings.json
rewrite is atomic on the same terms.

`load_config` also tightens an existing file to 0600 before reading the token
out of it, so a file left world-readable by an older installer or copied in by
hand is remediated on first use.

The environment fallback is kept and documented. It is the right answer on a
shared machine and in CI, and it still takes precedence over the file.

Empty optional values are dropped rather than stored, so a blank site ID at
install time does not shadow `MATOMO_SITE_ID` later. Relatedly, the writer no
longer unpacks a fixed four arguments: PowerShell 5.1 drops an empty string
argument to a native command, so a user who skipped the optional site ID
would have crashed the installer after typing the token. The uninstaller
removes the credential file and still clears the pre-v2.4.0 settings.json
entries, so an upgrade followed by an uninstall does not leave the old copy
behind.

Verified end to end against the local Matomo 5.13.0 container in a sandboxed
HOME: the installer wrote a 0600 file, left an unrelated settings.json key
untouched, `--check` read the file with no MATOMO_* in the environment and
probed the live instance, and the uninstaller removed both copies. The
extracted writer is also tested against a token full of shell and Python
metacharacters and against the dropped-argument case.
